## What this is for

The Rasch model gives every item the same slope, and the chess data have already turned up an item that doesn't go along: problem Y15, about as hard as Y29, whose success barely moves with skill. What happens when each item gets its own slope, and then its own floor and ceiling? This lesson builds that family, from the 1PL to the 4PL, asks what each new parameter costs and what the data can say about it, and fits all four to the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test. For that test my choice is the 2PL, and most of the lesson is the case for it.

## Goals

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- write down the 4PL, say what $a$, $b$, $c$ and $u$ do to a curve, and which constraints give the 3PL, 2PL and Rasch model;
- explain why the weighted score $\sum_i a_i x_i$ replaces the sum score under the 2PL, and why crossing curves give up specific objectivity;
- convert `mirt`'s intercept to a difficulty, and say how each model fixes the unit of the scale;
- explain why a lower asymptote is hard to estimate, and when a 3PL is a reasonable choice;
- fit all four models with `mirt` and compare them by BIC and by what they say about respondents.

## Core ideas

### One family of curves

One formula covers every model here. For person $j$ and item $i$,
$$\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = c_i + (u_i - c_i)\,\frac{\exp\big(a_i(\theta_j - b_i)\big)}{1 + \exp\big(a_i(\theta_j - b_i)\big)}.$$

- $b_i$ is the item's **difficulty**, its location on the $\theta$ scale.
- $a_i$ is its **slope** or **discrimination**: how quickly the probability rises as $\theta$ passes $b_i$.
- $c_i$ is the **lower asymptote**, the probability of success at very low ability; on multiple-choice items it is called the guessing parameter.
- $u_i$ is the **upper asymptote**; below 1, even the strongest respondents sometimes miss (a "slip").

"PL" stands for "parameter logistic", and the number counts the free item parameters. The Rasch model, a 1PL, frees only $b$ ($a = 1$, $c = 0$, $u = 1$). The 2PL frees $a$ and the 3PL frees $c$ as well, both from Birnbaum's chapters in [Lord & Novick (1968)](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL6568286W). The 4PL frees $u$ too ([Barton & Lord, 1981](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.1981.tb01255.x); [Loken & Rulison, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1348/000711009x474502)).

#### Try it: four parameters

```{ojs}
f_mid = (f_c + f_u) / 2
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 330, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Rasch (a = 1, c = 0, u = 1)", "This item"], range: [palette.light, palette.main]},

    Plot.ruleX([f_b], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(f_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{theta: f_b, p: f_mid}], {x: "theta", y: "p", r: 5, fill: palette.contrast})

```

```{ojs}

md`At θ = b = ${f_b.toFixed(1)} this item's probability is **${f_mid.toFixed(2)}**, halfway between the two asymptotes (dashed). ${f_c === 0 && f_u === 1 ? "With c = 0 and u = 1 that is 0.5, as in the Rasch model." : "It is no longer 0.5."}`
```

Move $a$ and the curve pivots around $b$; near zero it is almost flat. Raising $c$ lifts the floor, and lowering $u$ (the last slider) drops the ceiling. The point at $\theta = b$ always sits halfway between the asymptotes, so once $c > 0$ or $u < 1$, difficulty no longer means "the ability at which the probability is 0.5".

### What slopes cost: sufficiency and crossing curves

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Recall** from [The Rasch model](rasch.qmd): under the Rasch model the sum score $r$ is sufficient for $\theta$: patterns with the same sum score share an ability estimate. That lesson's widget broke this by switching to a 2PL.
:::

What takes the sum score's place under the 2PL? Write out one person's likelihood, as the Rasch lesson's Go deeper callout did:
$$\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_i \frac{\exp\big(x_i a_i(\theta - b_i)\big)}{1 + \exp\big(a_i(\theta - b_i)\big)} = \frac{\exp\big(\theta \sum_i a_i x_i\big)\,\exp\big(-\sum_i a_i b_i x_i\big)}{\prod_i \big(1 + \exp(a_i(\theta - b_i))\big)}.$$
The data meet $\theta$ only through the **weighted score** $\sum_i a_i x_i$, so under the 2PL it is sufficient ([Birnbaum, 1968](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL6568286W)). A correct answer counts in proportion to its item's slope. The weights are estimated item parameters, though; [Andersen (1977)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02293746) showed that a sufficient statistic free of the item parameters exists only under the Rasch model. Under the 3PL the lower asymptote spoils the factorization, and no simple statistic is sufficient.

#### Try it: which patterns share an estimate?

Five items ($b$ from −1.5 to 1.5; slopes 1, 2, 1, 1, 2). Pick a pattern; the table lists every pattern with the same sum score or weighted score, and each one's maximum-likelihood estimate of $\theta$ under the model you choose (in the 3PL, every $c = 0.2$).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ws_b = [-1.5, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1.5]
ws_a = [1, 2, 1, 1, 2]
ws_labels = ws_b.map((b, i) => `Item ${i + 1} (b = ${b}, a = ${ws_a[i]})`.replace("-", "−"))
viewof ws_x = Inputs.checkbox(ws_labels, {label: "Correct on", value: [ws_labels[1]]})
viewof ws_model = Inputs.radio(["Rasch", "2PL", "3PL (c = 0.2)"], {value: "2PL", label: "Model"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ws_pattern = ws_labels.map(l => ws_x.includes(l) ? 1 : 0)
ws_w = x => x.reduce((s, v, i) => s + v * ws_a[i], 0)
ws_est = x => ws_model === "Rasch" ? mle4(x, ws_b) :
  ws_model === "2PL" ? mle4(x, ws_b, ws_a) : mle4(x, ws_b, ws_a, ws_b.map(() => 0.2))
ws_sum = ws_pattern.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0)
ws_rows = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].flatMap(s => patternsWithSum(5, s))
  .filter(x => x.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0) === ws_sum || ws_w(x) === ws_w(ws_pattern))
  .map(x => ({pattern: x.join(""), "sum score": x.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0), "weighted score": ws_w(x), mle: ws_est(x)}))
  .sort((p, q) => p["weighted score"] - q["weighted score"] || q["sum score"] - p["sum score"])
Inputs.table(ws_rows.map(d => ({...d, "MLE of θ": Number.isFinite(d.mle) ? d.mle.toFixed(2) : (d.mle > 0 ? "+∞" : "−∞"),
  "": d.pattern === ws_pattern.join("") ? "← yours" : ""})), {columns: ["pattern", "sum score", "weighted score", "MLE of θ", ""], layout: "auto", rows: 14})
```

With the default pattern (only item 2 right) and the 2PL, five patterns have a weighted score of 2: `01000`, `00001` and the three pairs of slope-1 items, such as `10100`. All five share an estimate, −0.75, whether their sum score is 1 or 2, while `10000`, with the same sum score as yours, sits at −1.55. Switch to Rasch and the grouping goes back to the sum score. Switch to the 3PL and neither score is enough: the five patterns now spread from −1.09 down to −∞, since a lone correct answer is best explained as a lucky guess.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Recall** from [The Rasch model](rasch.qmd): specific objectivity asks that comparisons between items not depend on who takes them. With equal slopes, curves never cross, so one item is easier than another for everyone.
:::

Give two items different slopes and their curves cross where $a_1(\theta - b_1) = a_2(\theta - b_2)$: below that point one item is easier, above it the other. The 2PL buys its better description of items by giving up specific objectivity, and the chess data below show a crossing where most players sit.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz({
  q: "Under a 2PL, respondent A answers only one item correctly, with slope $a = 2$. Respondent B answers two items correctly, each with slope $a = 1$. Both took the same items and answered all of them. How do their ability estimates compare?",
  options: [
    {text: "They are equal", correct: true, why: "Both have a weighted score $\\sum_i a_i x_i = 2$, and under the 2PL the weighted score is sufficient. Which items they got right, and how many, doesn't matter beyond that."},
    {text: "B's is higher: B got more items right", correct: false, why: "That's the Rasch model's answer, where the sum score is sufficient. Under the 2PL each correct answer is weighted by its item's slope."},
    {text: "It depends on the items' difficulties", correct: false, why: "The difficulties enter the likelihood, but only in a term that doesn't involve $\\theta$. The estimate depends on the pattern only through the weighted score."}
  ]
})
```

## Go deeper: the weighted score under the 2PL, and why the 3PL has none

**Assumptions:** one respondent answers $I$ dichotomous items; responses are locally independent given $\theta$; the item parameters are known. Write $L_i = \text{logit}^{-1}(a_i(\theta - b_i))$.

**2PL.** The factorization in the main text puts $\theta$ and the data together only in $\exp(\theta \sum_i a_i x_i)$, so by the factorization theorem $t = \sum_i a_i x_i$ is sufficient. The score equation says the same thing: differentiating the log likelihood,
$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i a_i\,(x_i - L_i) = t - \sum_i a_i L_i,$$
so the MLE solves $\sum_i a_i L_i(\theta) = t$, which involves the data only through $t$. Conditioning on $t$ removes $\theta$, just as conditioning on $r$ did for the Rasch model. It buys little here: with slopes that are real numbers, nearly every pattern has its own weighted score, so the conditional distribution given $t$ usually has one pattern in it and nothing to estimate from.

**3PL.** Now $P_i = c_i + (1 - c_i) L_i$, and $\partial P_i/\partial\theta = a_i (P_i - c_i)(1 - P_i)/(1 - c_i)$. The same calculation gives
$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i a_i\,(x_i - P_i)\,\frac{P_i - c_i}{P_i\,(1 - c_i)}.$$
With $c_i = 0$ the last fraction is 1 and we're back to the 2PL. With $c_i > 0$ it is a weight that depends on $\theta$: near 1 for a person well above the item, near 0 for a person well below it, where a correct answer is mostly chance. Each correct answer's weight therefore changes with the ability at which it is evaluated, and no single function of the pattern carries all the information about $\theta$. That is the widget's 3PL result: a lone correct answer can leave the estimate at the bottom of the scale.
:::

### Reading `mirt`, and what fixes the scale

`mirt` ([Chalmers, 2012](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i06)) writes these models with an intercept, $\Pr(x = 1) = g + (u - g)\,\text{logit}^{-1}(a\theta + d)$; its `g` is our $c$ and its `u` is our $u$. Matching $a\theta + d$ with $a(\theta - b)$ gives $b = -d/a$, the conversion every chunk below uses. When $a$ is near 0, that ratio can be enormous, as the chess data will show.

What fixes the unit of $\theta$? The model only sees $a(\theta - b)$, so multiplying every $\theta$ and $b$ by $k$ and dividing every $a$ by $k$ changes no probability. The unit is a convention the software sets, as the origin was ([The Rasch model](rasch.qmd)): the Rasch fit fixes the slopes at 1 and estimates the SD of $\theta$; the 2PL fixes that SD at 1. A Rasch fit and a 1PL with one common, estimated slope are then the same model reporting different $a$ and $b$. That matters when reading output or comparing numbers across fits, the problem [Linking and equating](equating.qmd) takes up, but it says nothing about the data.

### What the lower asymptote needs

The lower asymptote describes people far below an item's difficulty. If few respondents are down there, the data say little about it, and a 2PL, with a lower slope and a shifted difficulty, can imitate a 3PL where the respondents are.

#### Try it: can a 2PL stand in for a 3PL?

```{ojs}
viewof la_c = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0.25, step: 0.01, label: "The 3PL's lower asymptote c"})
viewof la_mu = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Mean ability, relative to the item (b = 0)"})
```

```{ojs}
la_w = la_th.map(t => dnorm(t, la_mu, 1))

Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 320, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-5, 5]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["3PL (a = 1.2, b = 0)", "Closest 2PL"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(la_dens.filter(d => d.theta >= -5 && d.theta <= 5), {x: "theta", y: "d", fill: palette.light, fillOpacity: 0.5}),
    Plot.line(grid(-5, 5).flatMap(t => [
      {theta: t, p: p4pl(t, 0, 1.2, la_c), curve: "3PL (a = 1.2, b = 0)"},
      {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, la_fit.b, la_fit.a), curve: "Closest 2PL"}]), {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Closest 2PL, weighting by where respondents are (shaded): a = ${la_fit.a.toFixed(2)}, b = ${la_fit.b.toFixed(2)}. Over the middle 95% of respondents the two curves never differ by more than **${la_fit.maxDiff.toFixed(3)}**.`
```

As the widget loads, mean ability is 1.5, so the item is easy for most respondents. The curves differ by at most about 0.01 where respondents are, parting only to the left, where almost nobody is. Slide the mean ability down to −2 and the largest difference grows eight-fold, to 0.08: now many respondents sit near the floor, and the floor matters.

[Domingue et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-024-09977-2) looked at this through prediction. They simulated data from the 3PL and asked how much better a fitted 3PL predicted new responses than a fitted 2PL, using the IMV, a measure of predictive gain that [Model fit and out-of-sample prediction](fit-prediction.qmd) teaches. The average gain never exceeded 0.001, even with pronounced guessing in the generating model, and across 89 IRW datasets it averaged 0.00016. They connect this to the difficulty of identifying the 3PL's parameters ([Maris & Bechger, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1080/15366360903070385); [Haberman, 2005](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.2005.tb02001.x); [von Davier, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1080/15366360903117079)), noting that 3PL estimates may still flag items with guessing problems. A 3PL is a reasonable choice when the items are multiple choice, when a good share of respondents sits near chance, when the sample is large, or when $c$ is fixed or given a prior, as in [Guessing and priors](guessing-priors.qmd).

### The upper asymptote: ceilings and slips

What does $u < 1$ mean? That respondents far above an item's difficulty still sometimes miss it: through carelessness, a slip, or an item harder than it looks for experts. [Barton and Lord (1981)](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.1981.tb01255.x) added the upper asymptote to the 3PL in an ETS report; [Loken and Rulison (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1348/000711009x474502) estimated the 4PL with Bayesian methods and applied it to a delinquency scale.

The ceiling mirrors the floor: estimating $u$ needs many respondents far above the item, missing it now and then. Most data have few, so $u$ is weakly identified. On the RMET, the 4PL had not converged when EM stopped at its 500-cycle limit (below).

The same two asymptotes return, without a curve between them, in cognitive diagnosis. In the DINA model ([Junker & Sijtsma, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1177/01466210122032064)), a respondent who has every attribute an item requires answers correctly with probability $1 - s$, where $s$ is the item's *slip* parameter, and a respondent who lacks any of them with probability $g$, its *guess*. [Cognitive diagnostic models](cdm.qmd), an extension lesson, takes this up.

### Two philosophies

The choice between these models is also a choice between two traditions, which [Andrich (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1097/01.mlr.0000103528.48582.7c) describes as incompatible paradigms in Kuhn's sense. What does each assume?

- **The model comes first.** The Rasch tradition starts from what measurement should mean: a sufficient sum score, and comparisons that don't depend on which items or people were used ([Rasch, 1960](https://openlibrary.org/works/OL4506215W); [Wright, 1997](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3992.1997.tb00606.x)). It assumes items can be revised until they fit, and treats misfit as information about the items. It suits building an instrument you can still change.
- **The data come first.** The tradition that runs from Birnbaum through [Lord (1980)](https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203056615) takes the items as given and adds parameters until the curves describe them, accepting weighted scores and crossing curves. It suits analysing a test you can't change.

Some of the disagreement is about values, which data can't settle; some is empirical, and the RMET tests it below.

### Beyond four: asymmetric curves

All four models give point-symmetric curves. [Samejima (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02296149) proposed the logistic positive exponent family, which raises a logistic curve to a positive power so that it can rise slowly and then steeply, or the reverse. [Lee and Bolt (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-017-9586-5) study what asymmetry can say about item complexity, and the IRW's [asymmetric models vignette](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/vignettes/asymmetric_irt.html) fits such models across its tables.

## Simulate

The code below simulates 1,000 respondents answering 20 items from a 3PL with $c = 0.25$ on every item, then fits the Rasch model, the 2PL and the 3PL. It runs in your browser; the first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and `mirt` load, and the fits a little longer.

With the seed as written, the estimates of $c$ have a median of 0.25, right on the truth, but range from 0 to 0.48. BIC prefers the Rasch model (25,347, against 25,362 for the 2PL and 25,464 for the 3PL), although the 3PL generated the data. The three models' abilities correlate 0.97 to 0.99 with each other.

Now change `np`. At 300, the median estimate of $c$ drops to 0.06. At 10,000 (run that in your own R session), the estimates range from 0.07 to 0.42, BIC finally prefers the 3PL, and the abilities still correlate 0.99 or above. The lower asymptote needs a lot of data to settle; the abilities hardly notice it either way.


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
#| results: markup
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: true
#| label: unnamed-chunk-16
# Simulate responses from a 3PL with a lower asymptote of c = 0.25 on every item,
# fit the Rasch model, the 2PL and the 3PL, and see what each recovers.
# Adapted from ben-domingue/252: c4 (slide 61). Needs the mirt package.
library(mirt)
set.seed(1)
ni <- 20      # number of items
np <- 1000    # number of respondents (try 10000 in your own R session)
c_true <- 0.25

th <- rnorm(np)                  # true abilities
a  <- exp(rnorm(ni, 0, 0.3))     # true slopes, around 1
b  <- rnorm(ni)                  # true difficulties
pr <- c_true + (1 - c_true) * plogis(sweep(outer(th, b, "-"), 2, a, "*"))
resp <- as.data.frame(matrix(rbinom(np * ni, 1, pr), np, ni))

fits <- list(Rasch = mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE),
             `2PL` = mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE),
             `3PL` = mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE))

# mirt calls the lower asymptote g; in our notation it is c.
c_hat <- coef(fits$`3PL`, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "g"]
cat("Estimated c (truth 0.25): median", round(median(c_hat), 2),
    " range", round(min(c_hat), 2), "to", round(max(c_hat), 2), "\n")
cat("BIC:", paste(names(fits), round(sapply(fits, extract.mirt, "BIC")), collapse = "  "), "\n")

# Abilities: how well does each model recover the truth, and how much do they differ?
theta <- sapply(fits, function(m) fscores(m)[, 1])
print(round(cor(cbind(truth = th, theta)), 3))

plot(seq_len(ni), sort(c_hat), pch = 19, col = "#2780e3", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Item (sorted by estimate)", ylab = "Estimated lower asymptote c",
     main = paste(np, "respondents,", ni, "items"))
abline(h = c_true, lty = 2)

```

## Across the IRW

How much do slopes vary in real data? For each dichotomous IRW table with at least 250 respondents, 5 to 200 items and a nearly complete response matrix, [`compute.R`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/irw-course/blob/main/deepdives/1pl-to-4pl/compute.R) fits the Rasch model and the 2PL and summarises the slopes' spread by the SD of $\log a$, which rescaling $\theta$ leaves alone. It is 0 under the Rasch model, and 0.42 for the RMET above (0.43 in the corpus run's own sample).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
dd_path <- file.path("..", "deepdives", "1pl-to-4pl", "results.rds")
dd <- if (file.exists(dd_path)) readRDS(dd_path) else NULL
if (!is.null(dd)) {
  s <- dd$summary[order(dd$summary$sd_log_a), ]
  print(data.frame(table = s$table, items = s$n_items, respondents = s$n_resp,
                   sd_log_a = round(s$sd_log_a, 2), ratio_90_10 = round(s$ratio_90_10, 1),
                   BIC_prefers_2PL = s$prefers_2pl, converged = s$converged), row.names = FALSE)
  op <- par(mar = c(4, 1, 1, 1))
  known <- s$table %in% c("chess_lnirt", "wilmer-rmet-normative-data-set-2022")
  plot(s$sd_log_a, rep(0, nrow(s)), pch = 19, cex = 1.3, yaxt = "n", ylab = "", bty = "n",
       col = ifelse(known, "#c2410c", "#2780e3"), xlim = c(0, max(1.5, s$sd_log_a, na.rm = TRUE)),
       xlab = "SD of log slope within a table (0 = Rasch)")
  abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "#999")
  par(op)
}
```

Run on 24 September 2026: 6 tables fitted, 0 failed. In 5 of the 6, BIC prefers the 2PL to the Rasch model. The SD of log slopes runs from 0.28 to 1.42 (median 0.65); chess and the RMET are marked in orange.

This answers the Rasch lesson's question: are equal slopes plausible? The nearer a table's SD of $\log a$ is to 0, the more so. The IRW's [2PL discrimination vignette](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/vignettes/2pl_across_datasets.html) takes the question to its cognitive tables, slope by slope.
